title: Mineral Nutrition
tagline: The essential elements, their deficiency symptoms, and how plants obtain nitrogen from the soil.

overview.intro: Mineral nutrition is a short but precisely examined topic: which elements are essential and how that was proved, what each does, what happens when it is missing, how roots absorb ions against a gradient, and how nitrogen — the element plants need most of — reaches the soil. This chapter works through the criteria of essentiality and hydroponics first, then the macro- and micronutrients with their functions and deficiency symptoms, then absorption and the nitrogen cycle, and closes with nitrogen fixation, which is the biological answer to the hardest chemistry in the series.

facts.label: Sixteen essential elements
facts.value: Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur, iron, manganese, copper, zinc, molybdenum, boron and chlorine.

facts.label: Criteria of essentiality
facts.value: The element must be necessary for completion of the life cycle, cannot be replaced by another, and must be directly involved in metabolism.

facts.label: Hydroponics
facts.value: Growing plants in a nutrient solution without soil, which proved which minerals are essential.

facts.label: Nitrogen fixation
facts.value: The conversion of atmospheric N2 to ammonia by Rhizobium in root nodules and by free-living soil bacteria.

learningOutcomes: State the criteria that make an element essential and describe the hydroponic method.
List the macro- and micronutrients with the function of each and its deficiency symptom.
Explain how roots absorb mineral ions by active transport.
Describe the nitrogen cycle with its main processes.
Explain symbiotic and non-symbiotic nitrogen fixation and the role of the nodule.

learn.title: Essential elements and how they are studied

blocks.text: A mineral element is called essential only if it satisfies three conditions: the plant cannot complete its life cycle without it, it cannot be replaced in its function by another element, and it must take part directly in the metabolism of the plant rather than merely affecting the pH or the physical conditions of the medium. These criteria were established by working without soil. The culture solution method, or hydroponics, grows plants in a defined nutrient solution in which every component is known, with the roots supported by an inert material such as glass beads and the solution aerated because roots need oxygen for the active transport that takes up ions. To find which elements are essential, the technique of deficiency culture is used: plants are grown in a complete solution and then in solutions each lacking one element in turn, and the symptom that appears identifies the role of what has been removed. Adding the element back and seeing the plant recover completes the proof, since correlation must be confirmed by cure. Working in this way Arnon and Stout established the essential elements, and their list divides naturally. Macronutrients are needed in relatively large amounts because they are constituents of the molecules of life: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from air and water; nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur from proteins and nucleic acids; and calcium, magnesium and potassium, which serve as ions, activators and structural components. Micronutrients are needed in trace amounts, usually as the metal component of enzymes: iron, manganese, copper, zinc, molybdenum, boron and chlorine. The functional roles follow from where each element sits in a molecule. Nitrogen is in every amino acid, every protein, every nucleotide, chlorophyll and many coenzymes, so a deficient plant yellows because it cannot make chlorophyll or enzymes. Phosphorus is in nucleotides, ATP, membranes and the sugar phosphates of photosynthesis, so deficiency stunts growth and often gives a purplish colour from anthocyanin accumulation. Potassium is not part of any organic molecule yet is the chief inorganic cation, controlling stomatal opening, enzyme activation and the charge balance of the cell — deficiency shows as scorching of leaf margins. Magnesium sits at the centre of every chlorophyll molecule and activates many enzymes, so its deficiency mimics nitrogen deficiency but with interveinal yellowing in older leaves first. Calcium forms the middle lamella of cell walls and stabilises membranes; sulphur is in the amino acids cysteine and methionine and in several coenzymes; iron is needed for chlorophyll synthesis and as a component of cytochromes; molybdenum is required by the enzyme that reduces nitrate and by nitrogenase itself; and boron is needed for pollen tube growth and cell wall formation.

learn.title: Absorption of ions and the nitrogen cycle

blocks.text: Mineral ions enter the root by a two-stage process. The first is passive: ions present in higher concentration in the soil solution diffuse into the cell wall water of the epidermis and cortex, which is largely an affair of concentration and the electrical charge of the wall. The second is active and decisive: ions are taken from the dilute soil solution across the plasma membrane into the cytoplasm by carrier proteins, a process that consumes ATP and can accumulate an ion to a concentration many times that outside — which is why a plant cell sap is far more acidic and more concentrated than the soil water around it. The Casparian strip again plays its part, forcing the ions to cross a membrane at the endodermis so that the plant controls what reaches the xylem. Once in the xylem the ions are carried upward with the transpiration stream and distributed to the leaves, where they are incorporated into molecules. Nitrogen deserves separate treatment because although the atmosphere is nearly four-fifths nitrogen, plants cannot use it in that form: the triple bond of N2 is too stable to break without a catalyst, and the plant must receive nitrogen as nitrate or ammonium from the soil. The nitrogen cycle describes how that is maintained. Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N2 into ammonia or a related reduced compound, and it is carried out by free-living soil bacteria such as Azotobacter, by the symbiotic Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes, and by cyanobacteria such as Nostoc, as well as by lightning, which oxidises nitrogen in the air. Ammonification, or mineralisation, releases ammonia from dead organisms and excreta as decomposers break down their proteins. Nitrification converts that ammonia into usable nitrate in two steps: Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter oxidises nitrite to nitrate — both are chemoautotrophic bacteria that gain energy from the reaction and are sensitive to acidity and to waterlogging. Denitrification is the loss process: Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus in waterlogged, oxygen-poor soil reduce nitrate back to nitrogen gas, returning it to the atmosphere and reducing soil fertility — which is one reason drainage matters. Uptake, ammonification and fixation replenish the soil, so the cycle turns and nitrogen remains available for the next generation of plants.

learn.title: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation and the root nodule

blocks.text: The most important biological fixer in agriculture is Rhizobium, a bacterium that lives in the root nodules of legumes such as pea, gram, groundnut, clover and soybean. The partnership begins in the soil, where the legume root secretes flavonoids that the bacteria detect, and the bacteria reply with signalling molecules that cause the root hair to curl and entrapping them; the bacteria then enter through an infection thread formed by the plant, grow down into the cortex, and the plant cells divide to form the nodule, a specialised organ that did not exist before the infection. Inside the nodule the bacteria become bacteroids, and there they express the enzyme nitrogenase, which reduces atmospheric nitrogen to ammonia using ATP and electrons: N2 plus eight protons and eight electrons plus sixteen ATP gives two NH3, hydrogen and sixteen ADP. The ammonia is immediately converted to amino acids by the plant so that it never reaches a toxic concentration. The problem for the enzyme is that nitrogenase is irreversibly inhibited by oxygen, yet the bacteroids need oxygen for respiration to supply the ATP the reaction demands. The plant solves the paradox in three ways: the nodule wall restricts oxygen entry, the bacteria produce leghaemoglobin — which gives a pink interior to an active nodule — that binds oxygen and keeps its free concentration low while still delivering it to respiration, and the bacteroids are kept supplied with carbon from the plant’s photosynthesis. The exchange is therefore exact: the plant receives fixed nitrogen and the bacterium receives carbohydrate and a protected, oxygen-buffered home. Non-symbiotic fixers such as Azotobacter and Clostridium do the same chemistry in the soil without a host, and blue-green algae such as Anabaena in flooded paddy fields contribute as well. Practical consequences follow: legumes are grown in rotation or as green manure to restore nitrogen, and the failure of nodulation through poor soil pH, lack of the specific Rhizobium strain or waterlogging reduces yields — which is why farmers inoculate seed with the right bacterial strain before sowing.

learn.title: Applying mineral nutrition in the field

blocks.text: The applied side of this topic asks you to connect a symptom in a crop with its cause and its remedy, and the reasoning runs in a fixed sequence. First identify where the symptom appears, because that tells you whether the element can be mobilised: yellowing of the older leaves indicates a mobile element such as nitrogen, magnesium, potassium or phosphorus, which the plant has withdrawn to feed its new growth, while yellowing confined to the young leaves at the tip indicates an immobile element such as iron, calcium, sulphur or boron, which cannot be moved and so leaves the growing point short. Then identify the pattern within the leaf — uniform yellowing suggests nitrogen, yellowing between the veins with the veins staying green suggests magnesium or iron, purplish tints suggest phosphorus, and scorching of the margins suggests potassium. Only then propose the remedy, and a good answer proposes a remedy that matches the cause: a soil test first, because an apparent deficiency may instead be a locked-up element in the wrong pH, and only then a foliar spray for a quick correction of an immobile element or a soil application for a mobile one. The wider management questions follow from the nitrogen cycle. Legumes are rotated with cereals or ploughed in as green manure because their nodules fix nitrogen and leave the soil richer, which reduces the fertiliser the following crop needs. Nitrogen fertiliser is applied in split doses rather than all at once because nitrate is mobile in the soil and is lost to leaching and to denitrification in waterlogged ground, so a single heavy application washes away before the crop can use it. Drainage matters because the denitrifying bacteria that reduce nitrate to nitrogen gas thrive only where oxygen is absent, and liming matters because both Rhizobium and the nitrifying bacteria are sensitive to acidity — a sour soil loses fertility through the failure of its bacteria long before the plants show hunger. Hydroponic diagnosis completes the method: growing a affected plant alongside a healthy control in a complete solution, then removing one element at a time, separates a deficiency from a disease and identifies the element beyond doubt.

questions.prompt: State the three criteria that make a mineral element essential for a plant.
questions.answer: First, the plant must be unable to complete its life cycle without the element — a plant grown without it must fail to flower, set seed and produce a viable next generation, not merely grow more slowly. Second, the element must be indispensable in the sense that no other element can take over its function; if a substitute can perform the same role, the original is not strictly essential. Third, the element must be directly involved in the metabolism of the plant, taking part in a structural molecule, an enzyme reaction or an ionic process, rather than acting indirectly by altering the pH, the osmotic conditions or the physical properties of the medium. Meeting all three conditions is what placed the recognised macro- and micronutrients on the essential list.
questions.explanation: All three conditions with a line of explanation of each.

questions.prompt: Why can plants not use the nitrogen of the atmosphere directly?
questions.answer: The atmosphere is nearly seventy-eight per cent nitrogen, but the nitrogen exists as N2 molecules in which the two nitrogen atoms are joined by a triple bond. That triple bond is one of the strongest in nature, requiring a great deal of energy to break, and plant cells possess no enzyme capable of attacking it, so the gaseous nitrogen passes through the plant unharmed and unassimilated. Plants must therefore absorb nitrogen in a combined, reduced form — as ammonium or, more usually, as nitrate — which is present in the soil solution. The nitrogen cycle maintains that supply by converting atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia through fixation, releasing ammonia from dead matter through ammonification, and oxidising ammonia to nitrate through nitrification, while denitrification removes some again. The triple bond is thus the reason nitrogen fixation requires the specialised enzyme nitrogenase and the energy investment of the fixing organism.
questions.explanation: The triple bond, the absence of an enzyme in plants, the forms actually absorbed, and how the cycle supplies them.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between symbiotic and non-symbiotic nitrogen fixation with an example of each.
questions.answer: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation is carried out by a bacterium living in a close, mutually beneficial association with a plant: Rhizobium infects the roots of legumes such as pea and clover, forms nodules, and there fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which the plant uses to build amino acids while the bacterium receives carbohydrate and a protected environment. Non-symbiotic nitrogen fixation is performed by free-living organisms in the soil with no host: Azotobacter is an aerobic free-living bacterium and Clostridium an anaerobic one, and blue-green algae such as Nostoc also fix nitrogen independently, in flooded paddy fields for example. Both use the enzyme nitrogenase and both require energy, but only the symbiotic form supplies fixed nitrogen directly to a growing crop through its roots.
questions.explanation: Definition of each, an example of each, and the shared enzyme with the difference in association.

questions.prompt: Describe the nitrogen cycle in soil, naming the organisms and the chemical change in each step.
questions.answer: The nitrogen cycle maintains the supply of combined nitrogen that plants can absorb. It begins with nitrogen fixation, which converts the unreactive N2 of the atmosphere into ammonia: symbiotic Rhizobium does this within the nodules of legume roots, free-living Azotobacter and Clostridium do it in the soil, blue-green algae such as Nostoc work in flooded fields, and lightning provides a non-biological route by oxidising nitrogen in the air. Ammonification, or mineralisation, is the second supply route, in which decomposer bacteria and fungi break down the proteins and nucleic acids of dead organisms and of animal excreta, releasing ammonia into the soil. Nitrification then converts that ammonia into the form roots absorb most readily, and it occurs in two steps by two distinct chemoautotrophic bacteria: Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter oxidises the nitrite to nitrate; both gain energy from these oxidations and both are sensitive to acidity and to poor drainage. The nitrate now in the soil solution is taken up by root hairs by active transport and carried up the xylem, where it is reduced and assimilated into amino acids and so into the plant’s proteins. Denitrification is the counter-process: in waterlogged soil where oxygen is scarce, bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus use nitrate as an oxygen substitute, reducing it through nitrite and nitrous oxide back to nitrogen gas, which escapes to the atmosphere and removes fertility from the soil. Ammonification and fixation replenish what denitrification and harvesting remove, so the cycle turns and the soil remains capable of supporting the next crop.
questions.explanation: The five processes with organisms and chemical changes, the uptake step, and the closing balance of the cycle.

questions.prompt: A plant grown in a complete culture solution develops yellowing between the veins of its older leaves, while a second plant lacking iron develops the same yellowing only in its young leaves. Explain each symptom and state how the difference helps diagnosis.
questions.answer: Both plants show chlorosis — the failure to produce chlorophyll — but the position of the first symptom identifies the element, because it depends on whether the element can be moved within the plant. Magnesium is the element whose deficiency shows in older leaves first. It is a component of the chlorophyll molecule and, more importantly, it is mobile in the phloem: when the supply from the soil is short, the plant breaks down chlorophyll in its older leaves and translocates the magnesium to the young, still-growing leaves where it is needed for new chlorophyll. The older leaves are therefore sacrificed for the benefit of the new growth, and the interveinal yellowing appears in them first while the young leaves remain green. Iron behaves differently in two ways. It is required for chlorophyll synthesis itself — though it is not part of the molecule — and for the cytochromes of the electron transport chain, but it is immobile once laid down in the leaf: it cannot be withdrawn from older tissues and re-used. So when the supply fails, the older leaves keep the iron they already have and the young leaves, which depend entirely on fresh uptake, are the ones that cannot make chlorophyll. The symptom therefore appears first in the young leaves at the shoot tip. The diagnostic rule that follows is valuable in the field as well as the laboratory: a deficiency that appears in old leaves concerns a mobile element — nitrogen, magnesium, potassium or phosphorus — and points to mobilisation from storage, while a deficiency in young leaves concerns an immobile element — iron, calcium, sulphur or boron — and points to a failure of supply to the growing point. Adding the missing element back to the solution and seeing the chlorosis clear confirms the diagnosis, which is the second half of the proof that the element is essential.
questions.explanation: Both symptoms explained through mobility, the translocation argument for magnesium, the immobility of iron, and the general diagnostic rule with the confirmation step.

questions.prompt: Explain why nitrogenase cannot work in the presence of oxygen even though the bacteroids need oxygen, and describe how the root nodule solves the contradiction.
questions.answer: The contradiction lies in the enzyme and the metabolism of the same cell. Nitrogenase, the enzyme that reduces atmospheric N2 to ammonia, has an iron-molybdenum centre that is irreversibly oxidised and permanently inactivated the moment oxygen reaches it, so the reaction must effectively run anaerobically. Yet the bacteroid must respire aerobically, because the fixation reaction itself is enormously expensive — sixteen ATP for every molecule of N2 reduced — and only oxidative phosphorylation can supply ATP in that quantity. A cell that simply excluded oxygen would starve for energy; a cell that admitted it freely would destroy its own enzyme. The nodule solves the problem in three coordinated ways. First, the plant builds the nodule with a cortex that restricts the diffusion of oxygen inward, so the supply entering is limited. Second, the nodule contains leghaemoglobin, synthesised jointly by the plant and the bacterium, which binds oxygen with high affinity and keeps its free concentration at a very low level — low enough to protect nitrogenase — while still transporting it to the bacteroid’s respiratory chain, and it is this pigment that gives an actively fixing nodule its pink colour. Third, the bacteroid’s respiratory enzymes have an unusually high affinity for oxygen, so they can respire effectively at the low concentrations that leghaemoglobin permits. The plant further supports the arrangement by supplying sucrose from photosynthesis as the source of both ATP and reducing power, and by removing the ammonia at once and incorporating it into amino acids so that the product cannot build up and inhibit the reaction. The result is a compartment that runs an oxygen-sensitive reaction beside an oxygen-hungry metabolism — which is why a white or green nodule, lacking leghaemoglobin, is not fixing.
questions.explanation: The enzyme sensitivity and the energy requirement stated as the contradiction, then each solution — barrier, leghaemoglobin with its affinity, respiratory affinity, and the plant’s sugar and assimilation support.
